facts.statement: The study used a longitudinal design to track immune changes in five people with multiple sclerosis before and after their disease flares.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The immune profiles of the patients were compared against a group of healthy individuals.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Researchers separated different types of T cells, including those that have never seen an antigen, those that remember past infections, and those that regulate the immune response.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Before a flare-up, people with multiple sclerosis had a higher number of T cells specifically targeting the Epstein-Barr virus compared to normal levels.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: Following a disease flare, the number of T cells targeting the Epstein-Barr virus rose sharply in every category of T cells measured.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: T cells that could recognize multiple different viruses also showed high numbers before flares and expanded significantly after them.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The authors suggest that the rise in these specific immune cells happens at the same time as the disease flares and general immune system activation.
facts.subject: humans

facts.statement: The authors note that their small group of five patients is too limited to fully understand how these immune changes cause the disease.
facts.subject: humans
